idiom_name: Class.new + define_method built from the type table
implementation_notes: Ruby's class objects are already first-class values - each class is an instance of Class - so the paper's TypeClass/Class split is built into the language: a type is a Class created with Class.new (or a constant-assigned class), its shared behaviour is real methods added with define_method/class_eval from the type data, and every instance knows its type through obj.class and is_a?. The registry is a Hash of id => Class. Use this variant when per-type behaviour must be real methods, when is_a?/case dispatch should work, or when instances should be created with the ordinary .new. Its cost is the usual one for open classes: methods defined on a registered type are visible to every existing instance, and the type table is global state.
pitfalls: Class-level state inside the Class.new block (class instance variables, constants) is shared by all instances; per-instance data belongs in initialize.
An anonymous Class created by Class.new has no name until it is assigned to a constant (or given one), which makes error messages and inspect output useless for debugging a type table.
Because classes are open, reopening a registered type with class_eval changes every existing instance at once - the Ruby form of 'mutating the type object retunes the population'.

variants.name: Data.define value descriptor
variants.idiom_name: Data.define descriptor instance shared by typed objects
variants.implementation_notes: Since 3.2 Ruby has an explicit value-type constructor: Data.define(:id, :base_health, :attack) returns a class whose instances are immutable, value-equal carriers with with(**changes) for deriving a tuned descriptor - the data-shaped realization of a type object, and a much better fit than a Class when the types are loaded from files and only data varies. Instances of the domain object hold a reference to the descriptor (breed) and delegate; the registry is a Hash of id => descriptor. Choose this variant for data-driven catalogues; choose class-objects when per-type behaviour must be real methods, since a Data instance carries data, not methods defined from data (the block form of Data.define can add methods, but they cannot vary per descriptor).
variants.code_sketch:
MonsterType = Data.define(:id, :base_health, :attack)

registry = { "troll" => MonsterType.new(id: "troll", base_health: 48,
                                        attack: "The troll clubs you!") }

class Monster
  attr_reader :breed, :health
  def initialize(breed) = (@breed = breed; @health = breed.base_health)
end

elite = registry["troll"].with(base_health: 96)   # derived type, no recompile
pitfalls: A Data instance is frozen, but its members are not deep-frozen: a member holding an Array or Hash is still mutable and shared by every instance of that type.
Data instances are value-equal, so two descriptors with the same members are == ; registry lookups must key on the id, not on the descriptor.

MonsterType above is a class, not an instance - assigning the descriptor table to constants of the same name is an easy way to shadow the type class with a descriptor instance and get confusing errors.
